hook.support: Remember your first day somewhere new? You didn’t know where to go. You didn’t know who to ask. An induction pack fixes that. Now you get to write one.
hook.core: First day. You don’t know where the toilets are, who your supervisor is, or what to do if the fire alarm goes. An induction pack answers all of that before anyone has to ask. This is the boss mission for On the Job: you’ll build one for a real workplace.
hook.extend: An induction pack is a workplace’s first impression. It is also its first safety control. Building one pulls together all you’ve learned in this zone. You’ll mix three kinds of work writing. Then you’ll organise it so a nervous new starter can find things fast.

why.support: New workers get hurt most in their first months. A good pack helps keep them safe.
why.core: WorkSafe Victoria says young workers are most likely to be hurt in their first six months in a new job. A good induction is one of the best protections.
why.extend: Young workers are most at risk early in a new job. A clear induction is a legal duty for employers. It is also a real safety tool.

articles.title: Welcome aboard

body.support:
An **induction** is the welcome and training a new worker gets. An **induction pack** is the document that goes with it.

**Who is it for?** A new worker. They are nervous. They don’t know anyone. They don’t know the rules.

**What goes in it:**
- **Welcome:** what the business does.
- **Who’s who:** your **supervisor**, and who to ask.
- **Your first day:** when to arrive, what to wear, where to go.
- **Safety:** dangers, safety gear, and what to do in an **emergency**.
- **Your rights:** pay, breaks, and where to get help.
- **Steps:** how to do one or two key jobs.

**Make it easy to use:**
- Put a **contents page** at the front.
- Use clear **headings**.
- Keep sections short.
- Use dot points and numbered steps.
.
A new worker should find any answer in under a minute.
body.core:
An **induction** is how a workplace welcomes and trains a new worker. The **induction pack** is the document that goes with it: in print, online or both.

**Purpose and audience.** The purpose is to help a new worker settle in and stay safe. The audience is someone on their first day: nervous, new to the place and often young. WorkSafe Victoria says employers must give young workers the induction, training and information they need to work safely.

**What goes in it:**
- **Welcome:** what the business does and what it values.
- **Who’s who:** your **supervisor**, and who to go to for what.
- **Your first day:** start time, uniform, where to go, breaks.
- **Safety:** how to spot and report hazards, safety gear, first aid and **emergency** steps.
- **Your rights:** pay, breaks, payslips, and where to get help.
- **How we do it:** procedures for one or two key tasks.

That’s a mix of text types. Some parts are **informational** (facts to read). Some are **procedural** (steps to follow). Some are **organisational** (how the workplace runs).

**Make it easy to find things:**
- a **contents page** with section names and page numbers.
- clear **headings** and **sub-headings** (“Fire” beats “Other info”).
- short sections, dot points and numbered steps.
- the most important things (safety, who to ask) early.

**Test it.** Give it to someone and ask, “What do you do if the fire alarm goes?” Time how long they take to find the answer.
body.extend:
An **induction** introduces a new worker to a workplace: its people, rules, hazards and ways of working. The **induction pack** is the document behind it, and often the first thing a new starter reads.

**Purpose and audience.** Its purposes are to inform, to instruct and to protect. Its audience is a new, often young, worker who is anxious, overloaded with information and unlikely to read it all. WorkSafe Victoria says employers are responsible for giving young workers the induction, training and information they need to work safely.

**Typical sections:**
- **welcome:** what the organisation does and values.
- **who’s who:** the **supervisor** and key contacts.
- **first day:** start time, uniform, location, breaks.
- **health and safety:** spotting and reporting hazards, controls and safety gear, policies, first aid and **emergency** procedures.
- **rights and responsibilities:** pay, payslips, breaks and reliable sources of help.
- **key procedures:** one or two core tasks.

An induction pack is a hybrid. It combines **organisational** texts (how the workplace runs), **informational** texts (facts) and **procedural** texts (steps). Each part should use the features of its type.

**Navigation.** Readers rarely read a pack from start to end. They look things up. So it needs a **contents page**, informative **headings** and **sub-headings**, short sections, and safety-critical information placed early. Longer packs may need an index.

**Test it** by asking a new reader to find specific answers, and timing them. Every slow search shows a heading or section to fix.

caseStudies.title: The first six months

body.support:
**WorkSafe Victoria** looks after safety at work in Victoria.

In **February 2026**, it put out a warning to employers.

It said young workers are most likely to be hurt in their **first six months** in a new job. This includes **apprentices**. They are new. They don’t know the dangers yet.

WorkSafe said bosses must do more. They must train young workers. They must tell them how to stay safe.

WorkSafe says a good start covers:
- how to spot and report danger.
- the dangers at that workplace.
- the safety rules.
- first aid and emergencies.

An induction pack is one way to do this.
body.core:
**WorkSafe Victoria** is the agency that enforces safety at work in Victoria.

In **February 2026**, it urged employers to do more to protect **apprentices**. It said young workers are most likely to be hurt in the **first six months** of a new job. They are still learning the work and its risks.

WorkSafe runs a campaign for bosses called **“Would you work for you?”** It asks them to see their workplace through a young worker’s eyes.

WorkSafe says bosses must give young workers the training and information they need. A safety induction should cover:
- how to spot and report unsafe work.
- the hazards at that workplace, and how they are controlled.
- safety rules and procedures.
- first aid and emergencies.

Those are the core sections of a good induction pack.
body.extend:
**WorkSafe Victoria** is the state’s workplace health and safety regulator.

In **February 2026**, it urged employers to do more to protect **apprentices**. It said young workers, including many apprentices, have the highest chance of being injured in the **first six months** of a new job, while they are still learning the work and its risks.

Its employer campaign, **“Would you work for you?”**, asks employers to see their workplace through a young worker’s eyes. Would they feel safe, trained and able to speak up?

WorkSafe’s guidance says employers are responsible for giving young workers the induction, training and information they need to work safely. It lists four key parts of a young worker’s safety induction:
- an introduction to health and safety, including how to spot and report unsafe work.
- the workplace’s hazards and how they are controlled.
- safety policies and procedures.
- first aid and emergency procedures.

An induction pack turns that guidance into a document. But a pack only works if it is read, understood and backed by supervision. Young workers may not ask questions for fear of looking slow.

model.text:
**4. SAFETY**
**4.1 Hazards here**
The fryers and grill are hot all shift. Floors near the sinks get wet.
**4.2 Your safety gear**
Wear non-slip, closed shoes every shift. Use the heat-proof gloves on the fryer hooks.
**4.3 If there’s a fire**
1. Tell the shift manager straight away.
2. Leave by the nearest exit. Don’t stop for your bag.
3. Go to the meeting point: the far corner of the car park.
4. Wait there until the manager says it’s safe.
**Who to ask:** your shift manager, or Dani (Safety Rep).
why: Numbered sub-headings let readers jump to the part they need.
It moves from facts to read (4.1, 4.2) to steps to follow (4.3).
It ends by naming who to ask, so new workers aren’t left guessing.

rubric.start: Missing safety or who to ask.
rubric.great: Rights, reliable help and a procedure too.
Sub-headings, with safety near the front.

teacher.overview: The On the Job boss mission. Students build an induction pack for a new young worker at a chosen workplace, combining organisational, informational and procedural writing, organised with a contents page, headings and sub-headings, and pointing to reliable help. They test it with a timed “find the answer” test. The case study is WorkSafe Victoria’s February 2026 warning that young workers, including apprentices, are most at risk in their first six months, and its guidance on what a safety induction should cover.
prep: Collect a real induction pack or staff handbook (your school’s staff or student induction works).
Devices for writing the full pack.
Students should have done Rights at Work, Write the Procedure or Handle With Care first; the pack draws on all three.

**Annotation:** 1 organisational (who we are); 2 contacts early; 3 informational (first day facts); 4 sub-headings for navigation; 5 rights and reliable help; 6 procedural (steps); 7 sign-off record.

**Sort:** 7 am start — first day; fire meeting point — safety; payslips Thursday — rights; till and safe steps — how we do it; non-slip shoes — safety; Fair Work Ombudsman — rights.

**Case study:** young workers, including apprentices, have the highest chance of injury in their first six months, while they’re still learning the job and its risks; a safety induction should cover how to spot and report unsafe work, hazards and controls, policies and procedures, and first aid and emergencies.

realityCheck: **This is a big task.** The workbook holds the contents page and safety section; the rest goes on a device. Four sections are fine at support level.
**Students without jobs:** a sports club, a school canteen or a volunteer role works well.
**Avoid fake contacts.** Students should use roles (“shift manager”) or real agencies, not made-up phone numbers.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The timed test is competitive and shows why headings matter.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank and a four-section pack.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with six sections, text types, navigation and a timed test.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: hybrid text types, safety-critical ordering, numbered sub-headings and the limits of documents.
